On the same interval, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $79.22\%$ lower root mean squared error (RMSE) and a $10.40\times$ speedup over Euston (S\&P'~26) for QuickGELU. For SiLU, \SPA{}-accurate achieves $19.02\%$ lower RMSE and a $2.06\times$ speedup over THOR (CCS'~25).

title: DriveMind: Mind-Evolving Belief Tracking for Closed-Loop Autonomous Driving
author: Yan Shi
Kehua Chen
Jiarui Qi
Yihong Tang
Haichen Liao
Yinhai Wang
abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.

title: RADIANT: Object-Centric Feed-Forward Global Illumination
author: Sarah Zhang
Zhiyang Dou
Minghao Guo
Benjamin Tod Jones
Wojciech Matusik
abstract: Feed-forward neural renderers synthesize global illumination across novel 3D scenes without per-scene optimization or runtime ray tracing. Existing transformer-based renderers tokenize individual triangles, so self-attention scales quadratically with mesh resolution. Yet macroscopic radiative transport is governed by the underlying surface geometry and object arrangements rather than a particular mesh discretization; finer tessellation can thus inflate token counts without changing the underlying transport physics, motivating a discretization-agnostic and object-centric representation. We introduce RADIANT (RADiance-based Inter-Actor Neural Transformer), an object-centric architecture for feed-forward global illumination from point inputs. By representing each object with a compact budget of 32 surface-patch tokens, RADIANT decouples attention sequence length from polygon counts. In a single network, an inter-object scene transformer models 3D radiative exchange and a view decoder renders images at target camera poses. To capture light transport without materializing O(N^2) bias matrices, invariant form-factor attention embeds geometric distances and surface orientations directly into query-key dot products as SE(3)-invariant inner products weighted by learned area and material gains. For primary visibility without mesh connectivity, camera rays cross-attend scene tokens guided by depth-tested point splats in a shared spherical frame. Across a 1.03M-scene benchmark under matched model capacity, RADIANT reaches 25 dB tone-mapped PSNR in 5x fewer training steps than RenderFormer, and achieves 32.2 dB at 600k steps (+3.3 dB over RenderFormer and +7.6 dB over RenderFormer-V2). We further demonstrate the scalability of RADIANT, which completes a 512x512 forward pass of a 500-object scene in 0.83 s, with computational cost scaling with the number of objects rather than polygons.

title: Label-Budgeted Attribute Inference from Protected Features in Edge-Cloud Split Multimodal LLMs
author: Junguang Yao
Peichun Hua
Hanxiu Zhang
Yue Zheng
abstract: Edge-cloud split inference runs the early layers of a multimodal large language model (MLLM) on a device and sends intermediate features to a server to complete the task. While keeping raw images local is often perceived as a privacy benefit, an honest-but-curious server can still infer sensitive attributes, such as age, gender, and race, from the received features. Existing protections intervene at the input, transmitted representation, or model's responses, but their native evaluations rely on final-response refusals or fixed-classifier failures, which underestimate an adaptive server's capabilities. To address this, we propose a label-budgeted attribute-inference framework that measures representation-level privacy through a recovery curve: the share of the unprotected leakage the server recovers as a function of its labeled-sample budget, from zero (a classifier trained on unprotected features) to a full labeled set. Our evaluation across two popular MLLMs reveals two critical findings. First, in unprotected pipelines, intermediate features leak all three attributes regardless of the split depth. Second, even when protection mechanisms are deployed across different stages, sensitive information remains recoverable under limited label budgets. For example, Safe-LLaVA removes biometric content from the model's responses, but from the features it transmits in split inference, 20 labeled samples per class recover 75-85% of the unprotected leakage. This work provides a label-budgeted measure of feature-level privacy for split MLLM inference and motivates defenses that act on the transmitted representation.

title: AgentTrace: Execution-Level Fingerprinting of Black-Box LLM Agents
author: Gejian Zhao
Hanzhou Wu
Xinpeng Zhang
abstract: Verifying the provenance of autonomous LLM agents is a critical security challenge. Existing semantic attribution is easily obfuscated by system prompts, while active watermarking conflicts with schema-constrained tool generation. We propose AgentTrace, an active framework that identifies the foundation model behind a black-box agent via observable execution traces. AgentTrace injects structurally ambiguous probes to trigger tokenization-sensitive serialization failures at rigid tool interfaces. While these initial failures provide coarse-grained separation across model families, the temporal sequence of subsequent repair operations reveals fine-grained, model-specific recovery behaviors. By modeling these multi-step trajectories with lightweight Markov chains, AgentTrace achieves 96.0% attribution accuracy under adversarial identity spoofing. Crucially, sequential repair modeling successfully distinguishes the evaluated intra-family variants sharing identical tokenizers (e.g., Llama-3 8B/70B), substantially outperforming unordered behavioral statistics while remaining robust against prompt obfuscation and temperature scaling.

title: DiscoDemo: Discovering Efficient and Diverse Robot Demonstrations for Imitation Learning
author: Minho Park
Kinam Kim
Donghu Kim
Byungkun Lee
Dongyoon Hwang
Yongjae Shin
Junha Hyung
Hojoon Lee
Jaegul Choo
abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo

title: TTT in VLA Models: Exploring Training with Human Demonstrations
author: Qiangong Zhou
Jiafeng Liang
Yimin Dong
Yang He
Hongxiang Li
abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.

title: DELA: Learning Controllable Edits for Diffusion Language Models
author: Xinsong Feng
Chenan Wang
Leshu Tang
Johnny Liu
Dong Li
Da Li
Haipeng Chen
abstract: Diffusion language models (DLMs) support bidirectional denoising and iterative refinement, but generation remains largely controlled by token-level masking schedules. This leaves draft-level refinement implicit and limits explicit control over when to insert missing content, delete redundant spans, revisit uncertain regions, or stop editing. We introduce Diffusion Editing Language Adapter (DELA), a plug-in framework that enables controllable draft refinement with a frozen DLM. DELA operates on clean, variable-length drafts using four explicit editing actions: Insert, Delete, Remask, and Stop. The controller determines when and where to edit the draft, while the frozen DLM fills masked regions through denoising, separating high-level edit control from token-level generation. A naive single-phase editor would be computationally expensive because arbitrary interior edits can disrupt prefix stability and limit reliable KV-cache reuse. To address this, DELA uses a two-phase decoding procedure: a fast, append-only drafting phase that supports KV-cache reuse, followed by a global refinement phase that enables targeted non-monotonic edits to the full draft. We train the controller using a staged curriculum that begins with learning local edit priors from synthetic recovery tasks and mined actions that improve draft quality. Subsequent stages refine edit selection through rollout-based outcome preferences and alignment with downstream task feedback. Experiments on mathematical reasoning and code generation show that DELA achieves gains of up to 5.5 percentage points over direct diffusion decoding while keeping the backbone frozen. DELA thus provides a modular approach to explicit draft-level control in diffusion language models.

title: PRISM: Promoting Sampling Diversity of Large Language Models with Implicit Stochastic Modulation
author: Qixin Xu
Zihan Zhu
Xiaojiang Liu
Bohan Lyu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit mode collapse, where their output distribution concentrates on familiar semantic modes. When diversity disappears, repeated sampling becomes semantic repetition rather than discovery, making rare but stronger solutions unlikely to surface and leaving self-evolution and continual learning difficult to sustain. Most remedies intervene only at inference time, shaping sam- ples without making diversity a model capability. We propose PRISM, a training-time framework that internalizes diversity within the model. PRISM combines (i) submodular curation that pairs each prompt with diverse-yet-correct multi-teacher solutions, and (ii) stochastic embedding modulation, which turns special-token perturbations into implicit signals for sampling distinct outputs. A theoretical analysis establishes the stability of this mechanism. On WritingPrompts and BookMIA, PRISM moves the quality-diversity frontier outward, achieving the best generation quality in all model-benchmark settings while maintaining the strongest or near-strongest semantic diversity across two open-weight model families. It also improves sampling efficiency on math and code benchmarks. Beyond inference, PRISM yields a stronger foundation for reinforcement learning, sustaining diverse rollouts and mitigating the diversity collapse commonly observed during RL training.

title: Coupling Execution Horizon and Sampling Depth in Flow-Matching VLA Policies
author: Jiabing Yang
Yuan Xu
Yixiang Chen
Qisen Ma
Peiyan Li
Kai Wang
Chenhang Cui
Tao Yu
Zichen Wen
Wen Ye
Bowen Fang
Ziheng He
Xiangnan Wu
Yingda Li
Yan Huang
Liang Wang
abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/

title: Putting Transformer Theories to the Test
author: Awni Altabaa
Tobias Schnabel
Kiran Tomlinson
abstract: Several formal theories have been developed to characterize the capabilities and limitations of the transformer architecture, each employing different abstractions that capture different features of the architecture. Due to the differences in their underlying assumptions and conceptual frameworks, these theories can disagree in their predictions about what tasks transformers find easy or hard. We map out seven theories of transformer capability (Star-free, $\mathsf{AC}^0$, $\mathsf{TC}^0$, C-RASP, MPC, BAPO, and Sensitivity) and translate their results into a common matrix of predictions across a suite of tasks covering different computational structures. We provide new theoretical results to complete this matrix. We then evaluate theoretical predictions through controlled experiments measuring in-distribution sample complexity, length generalization, and pretrained language model performance. We find that no single theory explains the observed pattern of successes and failures. When a theory does not capture the transformer behaviors relevant to a task, its predictions break down; for instance, we show that the $k$-hop induction task is predicted hard by C-RASP because it does not model content-dependent attention, but we train small transformers on this task that length-generalize. Similarly, theories assuming hard attention like $\mathsf{AC}^0$ and BAPO predict binary majority to be hard, for which we also find success in practice. Together, our results point to several specific features that a theory of transformers must capture: soft rather than hard attention, dynamic content-dependent retrieval, bounded computation at each position, an account of learnability and inductive biases, and a combination of upper and lower bounds.

title: PersonaScienceBench: Evaluating Scientific Agents with Diverse Simulated Researchers
author: Siyang Wu
Weizhi Zhang
Chen Yang
Esther Xu Fei
Jorin Overwiening
Xu Pan
Jing Tang
Yixuan He
Kelvin C. Mo
Peiwen Li
Defu Cao
Xu Hu
Haixin Wang
Taoran Li
Haoming Li
Zheyuan Deng
Jingwen Zhang
Pengsong Zhang
Haichao Zhang
Guangze Luo
Yi Daniel Lu
Zihuai He
Chenxi Qiu
Dianzhuo Wang
Zhejian Peng
Shushu Liang
Wenyi Lu
Yifan Wang
Jintao Huang
Yijun Wang
Xiaomin Li
Yuexing Hao
abstract: Scientific agents collaborate with researchers whose expertise and preferences differ, but benchmarks usually hold the collaborator fixed. We introduce PersonaScienceBench: 200 tasks from five benchmarks across four scientific domains. Simulated researchers provide context and feedback according to persona profiles, while task objectives and grading remain fixed. Agents encounter researcher preferences only through conversation. Across eighteen modelconfigurations, task performance, fact recovery, and self-repetition reveal different strengths. Detailed GPT 6 Astra analyses show distinct agent responses across researcher profiles; interaction traces illustrate targeted clar ification and workflow revision. These behaviors can differ even when final scores match. PersonaScienceBench therefore evaluates how agents collaborate with diverse researchers alongside whether they complete the task.

title: Beyond What to Say: Proactive Utterance Timing with Inner Thoughts for Werewolf Agents
author: Yoshiki Tanaka
Shuya Uchiyama
Daichi Hamaguchi
Michimasa Inaba
abstract: Participating in a conversation involves not only deciding what to say but also whether to speak at all. This judgment carries even greater significance in environments like the Werewolf game, where participants' interests conflict, because both utterances and silence are subject to interpretation and assessment by others. Therefore, determining when to speak, as well as what to say, is crucial for an LLM agent playing the Werewolf game. In this study, we introduce a Werewolf AI agent developed for the Anytime Utterance Track of the AIWolfDial shared task. Our system builds on the existing Inner Thoughts framework, which determines utterance timing during conversations by generating internal thoughts and evaluating the value of each thought for expression at that moment. Since existing methods were designed for general dialogue, we have redesigned the system specifically for the competitive environment and incomplete information setting of Werewolf games. We call our adapted method Adversarial Inner Thoughts. Through experiments involving analysis of self-play logs and human evaluations, we analyze and discuss the effectiveness of our approach.

title: Context or Knowledge: How LLMs Attribute Their Own Answers
author: Kirill Afendulev
Alexey Dontsov
Alla Chepurova
Elena Tutubalina
Anton Korznikov
abstract: Language models can answer a question from a supplied document or from their parametric knowledge. When later asked where the answer came from, what determines their source report? We study this by intervening on the model's key-value (KV) cache after the answer is generated and before the source question is asked. On a controlled factual task with four models (7B-32B), changing or removing the document's cache never changes the report. In contrast, transplanting the question-and-answer (Q+A) cache between runs with identical question and answer tokens transfers it: every eligible report follows the donor, while the recipient's document is unchanged. On the two smaller models, steering Q+A values along directions fitted before any source question reverses 98.9-100% of reports across four document conditions at a fixed strength, while norm-matched random directions flip at most 1.1%. The components of keys and values along fitted directions carry the transplant effect: copying them alone nearly reproduces the report change; holding them fixed nearly prevents it. Applied during answer generation, the same value directions also change which source supplies the answer, though more weakly and depending on the prompt. Source reporting in this setting thus depends causally on cached state produced while answering. We do not establish general reporting accuracy or a complete interpretation of this state.

title: REACT: Representational Early Analysis and Control of Chain-of-Thought Trajectories
author: Hanwen Zhang
Enyi Jiang
Ruike Zhu
Qinan Yu
Sanmi Koyejo
abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) generation offers an opportunity to intervene before a reasoning model completes its answer. But does the point at which risk is easiest to detect also offer the most effective control? We study this question with REACT, a conditional activation intervention that learns a safety direction from paired safe and unsafe trajectories and applies it once to an early CoT hidden state. The model weights remain frozen, and all subsequent tokens are generated without further edits. To study timing, we train directions separately at each of the first five CoT positions and evaluate ungated edits with full post-edit regeneration. Across three distilled reasoning models and three generation seeds, the strongest gains concentrate in a two- to three-token early window; on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Llama-8B, the effect falls to approximately zero at the fourth and fifth tokens, even though later states can be more predictive of risk. This separates risk readability from effective control: intervention timing must be evaluated through its effect on subsequent generation. On the same 8B model, REACT raises the rate of fully safe CoT-answer outputs on StrongREJECT-273 from 29.06% to 82.05%, while keeping benign refusal and usefulness near baseline. An anonymized implementation is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/REACT_official2-333B.

title: Tampered ML: Evaluating LLM Judgment of Machine Learning Research
author: Soroush Ebadian
Parand A. Alamdari
Joe Benton
Hailey Joren
abstract: One approach to accelerating progress on AI alignment is to automate parts of alignment research itself. Doing so requires systems that can perform reliably on hard-to-supervise research tasks, including identifying flaws in research proposals and evaluating whether a proposed experiment supports its intended claim. To evaluate this capability, we introduce Tampered ML, a benchmark of 1,858 item-pairs, each consisting of an experiment proposal reconstructed from a published machine learning paper and a minimally edited counterfactual that introduces a targeted methodological flaw. Models must identify the more methodologically sound proposal in both presentation orders. A human validation study on a stratified sample estimates that 86% of items are valid (95% CI: 81-91%). Frontier models perform above chance but remain far from reliable (with Opus 5 achieving 77.9% accuracy). They are highly sensitive to the order of presentation and favor flawed designs that appear more specific, transparent, or conventional.

title: EDWARD-NMT: Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for Neural Machine Translation
author: Edward Nguyen
Thai Tran
Kiet Anh Hoang
Duy Hoang
Duy Vo
Khanh Le
Vu Le
abstract: Sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) is a powerful paradigm for scaling Neural Machine Translation (NMT) and managing language heterogeneity. However, practical limitations hinder its deployment on resource-constrained devices: the entire expert pool must remain in memory, and the per-token compute budget is statically fixed during training by rigid top-k routing. We introduce EDWARD-NMT (Elastic Dimensions With Adaptive Routing and Dual-consistency for NMT), a novel MoE encoder-decoder architecture designed for a train once, deploy anywhere paradigm that exposes a family of deployable sub-networks at inference time. EDWARD-NMT integrates three key innovations: (i) Matryoshka-style elastic dimensions to flexibly reduce the memory footprint; (ii) an adaptive sigmoid router with a learned, task-conditioned threshold, allowing each token to dynamically determine its active expert count; and (iii) a dual-consistency objective to maximize the performance of the extracted sub-networks. Extensive experiments on PhoMT (En-Vi), WMT-14 (En-De), multilingual OPUS-16, and a multi-domain De-En benchmark validate our approach. The full-capacity architecture matches or exceeds strong MoE baselines with improved parameter efficiency. Furthermore, the sub-networks seamlessly extracted from a single checkpoint consistently outperform comparably sized dense Transformers without any retraining.

title: ImageRSI: Verification-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Agentic Image Generation
author: Shuo Han
Zhilin Wang
Peng Ling
Wenjia Gong
Yang Liu
Guanjun Jiang
Yukun Cao
Xike Xie
abstract: Complex text-to-image requests remain difficult to satisfy reliably. Verifying and repairing an image can fix an individual output, but a successful repair does not necessarily carry over to other requests. We present ImageRSI, a framework that keeps the image generator frozen and combines three components: five-dimensional verification and repair within each task, an experience library shared across tasks, and offline updating of the judge. Candidate experiences enter the library only after paired A/B validation, and the judge is updated with supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on accumulated image-judgment records and evaluated before reuse. We also introduce ImageReq-Bench, a benchmark of 961 requests built around hard cases in real-world image-generation requests, each paired with an evaluation checklist. ImageRSI achieves a Checklist Strict Accuracy (CSA) of 52.6% on MindBench (with Nano Banana Pro as the generator) and 65.66% on ImageReq-Bench, and we compare system outcomes across judge-training configurations.

title: Semantically Rich, Metrically Affect-Blind: A Geometric Blind Spot in Modern Text Embedders
author: Mahdi Naser Moghadasi
abstract: We report a systematic dissociation in modern text embedders: sentiment is almost perfectly decodable from their embeddings, yet almost entirely absent from their metric. Across eleven frozen encoders spanning 2021 to 2026, including 2026-generation models and the 4B-parameter LLM embedder Qwen3-Embedding-4B, a linear probe recovers sentence polarity at up to 91.3% accuracy while cosine similarity separates polarity by a margin of only 0.003-0.064. Qwen3-Embedding-4B, the strongest probe in the panel, reaches 91.3% probe accuracy but only 64.3 retrieval MAP. Because retrieval, clustering, deduplication, and retrieval-augmented generation operate on the metric rather than on a trained probe, these systems are effectively blind to information their encoder demonstrably contains. A task-conditioning control suggests this reflects the pretraining objective rather than a prompting artifact: conditioning Jina-v5 on its classification task rather than its retrieval task recovers only about half of the MAP gain that injection achieves on the same weights (63.2 to 73.8, versus 85.1), and leaves the alignment gap essentially unchanged. Sentiment-Injected Sentence Embeddings (SISE) train a small (0.13M-0.69M-parameter) supervised-contrastive head on a frozen encoder in seconds on a CPU, using the labelled training set. The head improves every encoder released since 2022 on full-data probe accuracy (up to +5.8 points), retrieval MAP (up to +26.0) and polarity margin (7-61x). This is a specialization, not a free gain: the compact 128-d head loses 38-41 Spearman points on STS-B, while a fused variant that concatenates it with the base embedding loses 2.4-12.0. With the head, a 0.6B encoder at 128 dimensions matches a 4B encoder given the same head (91.8 vs. 90.3 MAP). We release a CPU-reproducible pipeline and a reusable diagnostic, the Attribute Alignment Gap.

title: MPQ: A Message-Passing View of Post-Training Quantization
author: Yanshuo Chen
Chenxi Liu
Reza Shirkavand
Heng Huang
abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) is a key technique for efficiently deploying large language models, as it compresses weights into low-bit representations without retraining. Existing PTQ solvers, including GPTQ, LDLQ, and block coordinate descent, commit each weight block to a single codeword before its neighbors are considered, leaving near-optimal alternatives unexplored. In this work, we cast row-wise PTQ as posterior inference over discrete codebooks, in which existing solvers correspond to a zero-temperature, hard-decision limit retaining only the top codeword per block. We propose Message-Passing Quantization (MPQ), which preserves soft posterior information across blocks during inference and commits to hard codewords only at the output stage. MPQ first uses vector approximate message passing to compute approximate blockwise posteriors, then refines a hard-decision initialization by exact block coordinate descent. Across 2-bit lattice and 3- and 4-bit scalar quantization on dense language models from Llama, Qwen, and Mistral families, MPQ improves perplexity and zero-shot accuracy over strong hard-decision baselines, and composes favorably with preprocessing techniques such as activation-aware scaling and incoherence processing. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/poseidonchan/MPQ.

title: From Noisy Retrieval to Decision Evidence: Silver Evidence Demonstrations for In-Context Learning
author: Masoud Monajatipoor
Fazlolah Mohaghegh
Hamid Reza Hassanzadeh
Akash Uttamrao Bhoite
Robert E. Tillman
abstract: RAG and retrieval-augmented few-shot ICL can struggle when decision-relevant evidence is buried in long, noisy context. Retrieved passages and demonstrations may contain redundant or distracting information. Although expert-labeled development examples may identify the text supporting each decision, these annotations are typically used only as answer-side rationales rather than as supervision for filtering noisy retrieval. We propose silver-evidence demonstrations, which replace raw retrieved passages in ICL examples with generated, target-conditioned evidence summaries. For each labeled development example, an LLM generates silver evidence without access to the expert label or gold evidence; this evidence is then paired with the expert label and gold evidence where available. At test time, a single structured call generates silver evidence from retrieved passages and then predicts the final label and decision evidence. Across EI 2.0, SciFact, synthetic policy retrieval, and HICRIC/IMR data, our full method improves over equally sized gold-only ICL (label-only for policy) on three of four datasets and improves evidence F1 on all annotated datasets. It also achieves higher mean label accuracy than InstructRAG-style ICL on all four datasets. These results suggest that replacing demonstration-side retrieved passages with compact, target-conditioned silver evidence is particularly useful for decisions based on long and noisy text, where it reduces distracting context while preserving decision-relevant signals and expert supervision.

title: Shorter Is Not Cheaper: A Controlled Comparison of Declarative Animation Specifications and Free-Form Code for LLM-Generated Explanations
author: Jiantang Huang
abstract: Chat assistants increasingly answer conceptual questions with interactive, animated explanations, generated either as free-form HTML/JavaScript or as declarative specifications that a fixed runtime plays. The declarative route is widely expected to be cheaper, faster and more reliable, because its outputs are shorter and constrained. We test this expectation in controlled comparisons whose hypotheses and analysis plans were frozen before the runs. We designed ExplainSpec, a time-indexed declarative animation format, and an observation contract that makes every generated explanation programmatically inspectable; validated, pacing-agnostic checkers score 20 explanation requests from five domains. Three Claude models (360 jobs) and, in a follow-up, the open-weight Qwen3-14B with thinking enabled and disabled (240 jobs) answered every request in both formats. For every model the specifications were 25-48% shorter in answer tokens (output excluding reasoning), yet with reasoning enabled total output fell significantly only for the largest Claude model and no model generated significantly faster. The reasons differed. The Claude models reasoned far more before writing specifications (exploratory; for the two larger models, from 15-20% to 85-88% of generations). Qwen3-14B reasoned about as much in both formats (a pre-registered test of this shift was not supported), and its shorter answers saved little against a reasoning trace more than twice as long. Nor were specifications more reliable: free-form pages were valid after one repair round in 95-100% of jobs for every model, whereas Qwen3-14B produced valid specifications in only 33% of jobs and passed all semantic tests in 17% (HTML/JavaScript: 62%). For reasoning models, a shorter format alone therefore does not make generation cheaper, faster or more reliable, and a format learned in context can cost reliability.

title: TravSUITE: Traversability via Self-Supervised, Uncertainty-Aware IRL and Terrain Estimation
author: Samuel Triest
Amirreza Shaban
David D. Fan
Wenshan Wang
Sebastian Scherer
abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.

title: SyncPro: Synchronous Reasoning and Responding for Proactive Streaming Video Understanding
author: Xueyun Tian
Bingbing Xu
Jiaming Liu
Jinpeng Yu
Yang Shi
Yu Zhao
Ruihua Huang
Yuanzhuo Wang
Huawei Shen
abstract: Proactive streaming video understanding requires assistants to track unfolding events and respond when a user's requested condition is met. To make these decisions, assistants must accumulate relevant evidence and reassess response conditions as new observations arrive. Existing work offers complementary capabilities for this process: proactive video assistants learn when to respond, while streaming video reasoning methods generate scheduled intermediate text to organize observations and support subsequent answers. Together, these capabilities provide a foundation for proactive reasoning, but how to coordinate ongoing reasoning with timely responses remains underexplored. In a direct adaptation, fixed reasoning intervals can trigger updates when nothing relevant has changed or postpone useful updates until the next scheduled step. Sharing one generation path also couples two distinct requirements: preserving evidence for future decisions and producing only the response requested by the user. Moreover, responses generated after reasoning must wait for it to finish, even when sufficient evidence is already available. To address these challenges, we introduce SyncPro, a synchronous dual-stream framework with specialized generation paths for evidence tracking and user-facing responses. Its Inner and Response branches share causal history and activate independently, allowing relevant evidence changes to trigger internal updates and responses to proceed concurrently with ongoing reasoning. We construct 189K dual-stream examples and train SyncPro through supervised fine-tuning followed by trajectory-level reinforcement learning. Experiments across three proactive benchmarks show improved response timing and more accurate answers to user requests.

title: Beyond Data Schedule: Fast LLM Pretraining on Data Mixtures by Loss-Reweighting
author: Jiazheng Li
Huaqing Zhang
Jing Xu
Tianle Cai
Jingzhao Zhang
abstract: Large language models often acquire specialized capabilities through successive pretraining stages, but these gains can come at the cost of forgetting earlier knowledge. In this work, we investigate whether such trade-offs can be improved by changing how strongly each domain contributes to learning while keeping its data exposure fixed. We find that, in controlled knowledge--mathematics experiments, loss reweighting produces a single checkpoint that surpasses the best knowledge and reasoning scores attained along either stage trajectory. This reveals an independent control that data-mixture ratios alone do not capture. Building on this finding, we propose LARE (Loss-Adaptive Reweighting under fixed Exposure), which automatically adjusts domain weights from running loss statistics. Motivated by a theoretical analysis of gradient noise, its normalized inverse-square-root rule balances relative loss scales without changing the sampled mixture or requiring additional runs to search for weights. Across knowledge, mathematics, and code, \Method{} improves all five evaluated benchmarks for a 1.5B model trained on 240B tokens, averaging +7.84 pp over a matched direct mixture, including gains of +17.06 pp on GSM8K and +9.00 pp on MATH. These findings demonstrate that adjusting domain loss scales can improve joint capabilities without additional domain exposure.

title: Rethinking LoRA Initialization for Robust Asymmetric Learning Rates
author: Disen Liao
Yaoliang Yu
abstract: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $\eta_B / \eta_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. Under standard \initA, the update contains an initialization-induced noise term whose magnitude can be affected by the LR for $B$, $\eta_B$, the initialization scale $\beta$, and the adapter rank $r$. In practical LLM fine-tuning, this non-vanishing noise can limit the performance gains expected from LoRA+ style asymmetric LRs. To suppress this effect, we propose \initAA, a simple initialization that scales the variance of $A$ as $\sigma_A^2 \propto n^{-2}$ while keeping $B_0=0$. Under matched rank and training time for both initializations, this reduces the initialization-noise energy by an additional factor of $1/n$, stabilizing asymmetric LoRA training while preserving zero initial adapter output. Empirically, \initAA substantially widens the stable LR region across initialization scales, adapter ranks, and LoRA update multipliers. Across tasks and models, \initAA reduces best-ratio drift, prevents the high-ratio collapse observed with standard \initA, and makes the width-based guideline $\eta_B \approx n \eta_A$ a useful starting point for finite pretrained models.

title: Geometry-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Close-Fitting Wearable Insertion
author: Takuma Tsukakoshi
Elle Miller
Tamon Miyake
Namiko Saito
Yushi Wang
Shigeki Sugano
Tetsuya Ogata
Sethu Vijayakumar
abstract: Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion. We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7 +- 1.2% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/20 real-robot trials.

title: Separating Angular Alignment from Radial Ordering in Hyperbolic Vision-Language Models
author: Mingyang Gao
Yuwei Wu
Shiyu Luo
Wei Wu
Xiaomeng Fan
Qihao Lv
Haoyu Zhang
Rui Gao
Bingzhen Liu
Zhi Gao
Che Sun
abstract: Hyperbolic vision-language models are well suited to modeling the hierarchical structure of multimodal data, because hyperbolic volume grows exponentially with radius, enabling low-distortion representations of tree-like taxonomies from general to specific concepts. However, existing pretraining objectives for hyperbolic vision-language models entangle semantic alignment with entailment modeling, forcing radial coordinates to simultaneously encode semantic matching and hierarchical structure, leading to conflicting geometric constraints. In this paper, we introduce AURORA, a hyperbolic vision-language framework that decouples the objectives through angular alignment and a novel Radial-Angular Order Cone (RAOC) for entailment modeling. Angular alignment captures semantic similarity while preserving the radial structure for representing hierarchies. Unlike conventional entailment cones, RAOC determines angular allowance from relative parent-child radial gaps. It is incorporated into hierarchical entailment contrastive training to capture partial-order relations. We further introduce a norm regularization term that prevents undesirable radial degeneration for stable training. We train models on millions of image-text pairs and evaluate them across zero-shot classification, image-text retrieval, hierarchical reasoning, and compositional understanding. Our model consistently outperforms strong Euclidean and hyperbolic vision-language baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of decoupling semantic alignment from hierarchical entailment modeling.

title: Covariance-Informed Ensemble Score Filtering: Embedding Localized Covariance Geometry into Score-Based Transport
author: Siming Liang
Peter Jan van Leeuwen
Hristo G. Chipilski
Zezhong Zhang
Feng Bao
Guannan Zhang
abstract: Background-error covariance models are central to atmospheric data assimilation because they spread partial observational information across space, variables, and dynamically coupled scales. Ensemble and variational methods exploit this covariance geometry efficiently, but their standard analysis formulations are largely built around Gaussian or locally quadratic approximations. Score-based ensemble filtering provides a framework for nonlinear distributional transport, but existing Ensemble Score Filter (EnSF) formulations lack an intrinsic covariance-mediated pathway for propagating likelihood information from observed to unobserved state components. We introduce a covariance-informed ensemble score filter (CI-EnSF) that embeds localized forecast-error covariance geometry directly into the forward diffusion and reverse transport. The proposed forward diffusion is covariance-shaped in standardized state space and becomes isotropic under the corresponding control-variable transformation. This covariance structure continuously propagates observational information from observed to unobserved state components throughout the reverse transport analysis trajectory. Experiments with Lorenz-96 and surface quasi-geostrophic (SQG) dynamics show a clear regime dependence. For linear observations, a well-tuned LETKF is more accurate, while CI-EnSF maintains stable cycling and effective covariance-mediated information propagation. Under strongly nonlinear observations and under climatological initialization, CI-EnSF achieves lower analysis error and greater cycling robustness than Gaussian ensemble benchmarks such as the LETKF, with improvements extending across spatial scales in the nonlinear SQG experiment. These results suggest that the principal benefit of CI-EnSF arises from combining nonlinear distributional transport with the mature covariance geometry used in conventional data assimilation.

title: From Promises to Accountability: Comparative AI Modeling and Visualization of Electoral Commitments in Nepali Political Texts
author: Prakash Poudyal
Nischal Karki
Amrit Dahal
Rajani Chulyadyo
Sameer Tamrakar
Bal Krishna Bal
abstract: Election Commitment Mining refers to the analysis of election commitments made by electoral candidates or political parties during election campaigns. However, many elected candidates and political parties, especially in developing South Asian countries, do not fully deliver on the promises they make before elections. Even after the elections, commitments presented through election manifestos, posters, pamphlets, videos, and other campaign materials are often not systematically or transparently archived. As a result, these promises tend to fade away over time, making it difficult to hold the elected candidates accountable for their commitments. To address this persistent issue, this research aims to develop a system capable of structuring the commitments made by candidates during election periods. In this work, we created the first gold-standard dataset of Nepali political texts (Cohen's kappa = 0.777) and evaluated machine learning, deep learning and large language models to automatically extract and analyze election commitments. LaBSE-LR achieved the best results among machine learning models (0.897 accuracy, 0.896 macro F1-score, 0.947 AUROC), while fastText-LSTM achieved the highest performance among deep learning models (0.914 accuracy, 0.913 macro F1-score, 0.961 AUROC). Among the three evaluated large language models, Qwen3-8B performed best in the few-shot setting (0.848 macro F1-score). The outcome of this work is integrated into a mobile application, where commitments can be visualized with the support of GAI, enhancing transparency, civic engagement, and electoral accountability.

title: Sparsity-driven emergence of functional modularity in multitask neural networks
author: Bowen Shi
Qi Ouyang
Long Qian
abstract: Neural networks can learn multiple tasks, but how learning organizes shared computation into specialized and reusable components remains poorly understood. In this work, we show that sparsity inducing regularization promotes functional modularity in multitask networks without predefined module boundaries. Using functional profiling in multilayer perceptrons and a lightweight transformer, we identified compact, task-selective subnetworks, termed functional tokens. Across rule-based task families, selectively retaining these tokens preserves their associated functions while reducing performance on other tasks. Such specialization develops preferentially in deeper layers during training, while earlier layers retain shared computation. Regularization strength and form shape module compactness and specialization, while task weighting alters functional allocation. Moreover, extracted functional tokens can be recombined through alternative pathways to reconstruct a learned composite computation without retraining, preserving their connectivity and learned weights. Our results suggest that sparsity-constrained optimization shapes not only parameter use but also the organization and reuse of learned computation.

title: Detecting Insecure Compositions of Clean Agent Skills via Capability-Flow Graph Analysis
author: Yihao Li
Chuanpu Fu
Yizhou Zhao
Miao Chen
Qi Li
Ke Xu
abstract: AI agents increasingly extend their capabilities by invoking third-party skills, where each skill encapsulates instructions, scripts, and resources for agents to execute on demand. This paper reveals that deploying many benign skills together introduces compositional security risks: multiple individually clean skills can compose into safety-violation chains, because the agent passes an upstream skill's output to a downstream skill's input across invocations. The risk arises not from any single skill, but from the agent's runtime orchestration, and thus cannot be captured by existing malicious skill detection methods. To this end, we develop KnotScryer to detect insecure skill compositions by treating skills as typed capability flows. In particular, we abstract each skill into a capability summary, and construct the Skill Capability-Flow Graph (SCFG), where edges denote cross-skill information flow. Moreover, we design a search policy that tracks protected or untrusted data along handoff edges to locate paths reaching insecure operations. Finally, a two-layer verification method replays the insecure information flow for reachability analysis and applies a task-anchored LLM chain audit to confirm the semantic plausibility of the identified violation chains. We deploy KnotScryer to analyze 13,598 clean skills from ClawHub, and validate the detected chains across three agent frameworks and three LLMs. KnotScryer identifies 612 insecure compositions, which are consistently exploited across agent frameworks. Meanwhile, under GLM-5.1, it outperforms tag-match and graph-only baselines by improving the exploitation rate from 16.5%-18.2% to 85.6%, while reducing the search space by 85.3%. Furthermore, 13.7% of the detected chains consist entirely of skills labeled safe by a single-skill scanner, showing that KnotScryer effectively identifies insecure compositions that per-skill auditing cannot.

title: Playing Bias: Epistemic Games for Interpreting Text-to-Image Models
author: Amalia Foka
abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) systems do not merely render prompts; they circulate defaults for "what X looks like," shaping recognition through pose, camera, costume, props, and setting. While technical audits quantify disparities, they rarely cultivate the literacy needed to argue how images assemble stereotypes and confer authority. This paper translates a three-stage, humanities-informed framework into a set of epistemic games that make this cultural work visible and debatable: Interpret (art-historical close looking with AI outputs), Interrogate (counter-intent prompting as artistic exploration), and Expose (creative misuse through paired prompts with a constant motif and a BiasSlot rule, in which only the bias cue varies). In a pilot with undergraduate fine-arts students, the games shifted discussion from impressionistic reactions to concise, warranted hypotheses grounded in visual evidence, supported by lightweight classroom instruments that enabled reproducibility and structured collaboration. We argue that such game-based approaches foster critical literacy across educational contexts, equipping learners to recognize, discuss, and contest how T2I models encode bias.

title: PersonalQuery-Benchmark:Evaluating Retrieval Robustness to Personalized User Expression Differences
author: Wenyu Liang
Hongzhi Yin
Tongtong Wu
Fan Liu
Kexin Dai
Weiqing Wang
abstract: Existing personalized information retrieval methods mainly model differences in user needs through user preferences and query intent, while paying little attention to the personalized expression differences that arise when different users express the same retrieval need. Existing real query data typically lack stable user identities, long-term expression histories, and intent-matched counterparts, making it difficult to systematically evaluate the impact of personalized expression differences on retrieval outcomes. To this end, we propose PersonalQuery-Benchmark (PQB). PQB models personalized syntactic expression and personalized writing errors from users' historical texts, constructs personalized syntactic expression queries and personalized writing-error queries, and validates benchmark quality through LLM assessment and independent human evaluation. PQB covers three Amazon product domains with 6,516 query instances in total, and is evaluated on five retrieval models representing lexical, learned sparse, dense bi-encoder, late-interaction, and hybrid architectures, together with two LLM-based ranking models. Results show that even when the information need is held fixed, personalized expression differences still induce measurable ranking variation; different retrieval models exhibit clearly different sensitivities to syntactic variation and writing-error variation, while higher overall retrieval effectiveness does not necessarily correspond to stronger robustness against expression variation. PQB provides a new benchmark and evaluation framework for systematically studying personalized expression robustness. The associated code and dataset are available at the following address: https://github.com/cpxjazz123/PersonalQuery-Benchmark.

title: $Î¨$-0.6: Adaptive Streams of Thought in a Unified Vision-Language World Model
author: Khai Loong Aw
Klemen Kotar
Baihan Zhang
Yifan Liu
Lilian Chen
Atlas Kazemian
Rahul Venkatesh
Daniel Yamins
abstract: Humans reason about the physical world by flexibly combining different forms of inference as a problem unfolds. Achieving this flexibility is a major open challenge in AI: capabilities often remain separated across specialized models, limiting how they can be composed and jointly adapted to a task. We introduce $\Psi$-0.6, a unified vision-language world model that adaptively composes perception, language, geometry, and simulation within a shared reasoning process we call streams of thought. These streams interleave images, text, and explicit representations of geometry and motion, all of which the model can generate and interpret through a shared token interface. $\Psi$-0.6 surpasses leading open-weight models zero-shot on multi-view spatial reasoning, with further gains from reasoning through geometric intermediates. It also supports counterfactual simulation: generating and interpreting imagined scenes to determine, for example, whether moving an object would obstruct a pathway. Reinforcement learning from task feedback jointly optimizes the selection, generation, and use of intermediate representations, improving visual question-answering accuracy with gains that transfer to unseen benchmarks. $\Psi$-0.6 offers a path toward adaptive physical reasoning -- not only predicting the physical world but also choosing the representations through which to reason.

title: Not All Information Is Worth Asking For: Decision-Informed Information Seeking with LLMs
author: Seunghan Lee
Jun Seo
Junhyeok Kang
Jaehoon Lee
Sangjun Han
Sungdong Yoo
Minjae Kim
Tae Yoon Lim
Dongwan Kang
Hwanil Choi
Soonyoung Lee
Wonbin Ahn
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to support decisions under incomplete information, where deciding what to look up and when to stop matters as much as the final answer. However, LLMs fall into an information trap: They pay for checks, i.e., costly pieces of evidence, that cannot change their decision or are not worth their cost, and they keep asking when the evidence is already sufficient. To this end, we propose Decision-Informed Value-of-information Acquisition (DIVA), a simple yet effective procedure for LLM information seeking based on the decision value of evidence. DIVA 1) lets the LLM specify a small decision model, i.e., how likely a bad outcome is and how each check would shift this probability, through short numeric questions and 2) values each candidate check by how much its imagined outcomes improve the decision net of its cost, stopping when no check is worth its cost. Its variant, DIVA-U, further accounts for the LLM's uncertain estimates of how strongly each check shifts this probability. DIVA is training-free and applies to any LLM. Across four domains and 20 LLMs, DIVA-U has lower regret, i.e., value lost relative to the best possible decision, than every LLM baseline on real-world data, mainly by stopping once evidence suffices, and DIVA cuts the regret of the best LLM baseline by 75% in synthetic scenarios where every check's reliability is given. Code: http://github.com/seunghan96/diva.

title: Depth-Dependent Safety Geometry in Vision-Language Models: Layer-Wise Localization and Bidirectional Refusal Control
author: Muhammad Zeeshan Karamat
Syed Talal Hassan
Christiana Chamon Garcia
abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are widely deployed, yet the internal mechanisms behind their safety behavior remain poorly understood. We present a lightweight inference-time framework for localizing and manipulating safety-sensitive representations in frozen VLMs, without retraining or modifying parameters. On Qwen3-VL-4B, layer-wise activation divergence analysis reveals non-uniform safety geometry across depth. Causal interventions show that early vision layers support strong bidirectional refusal control through activation steering along a learned safety direction, with unsafe rejection spanning 6%-96%, whereas later layers respond more to activation magnitude scaling and exhibit a substantial safety-selectivity trade-off. Deeper layers remain well separated along the safety direction yet are largely insensitive to steering, distinguishing representational separability from causal controllability. InternVL2.5-4B shows qualitatively similar depth-dependent activation geometry despite differences in layer location and magnitude. Our results expose a white-box, representation-level refusal-bypass attack surface in VLM vision encoders and motivate inference-time stabilization of safety-sensitive representations.

title: Freeform Programmable Liquid Crystal Elastomers via Monolithic Integration of Co-Optimization and 4D-Printing
author: Yibo Wang
Asad Farooq Ahmed
Weichen Li
Weiyun Xu
Xiaojia Shelly Zhang
abstract: Liquid crystal elastomers (LCEs) are active materials capable of large, reversible thermally induced actuation, offering significant potential for applications such as artificial muscles and soft robotics. However, their broader deployment is hindered by the lack of a unified design-to-fabrication framework, the strong coupling among geometry, director fields, and manufacturing constraints, and the difficulty of reliably translating complex designs into physically realizable architectures. Here, we present an autonomous and monolithic integration of co-optimization and 4D printing that enables the end-to-end design-to-realization of versatile programmable LCE architectures with superior precision, complexity, and versatility. The proposed framework establishes a unified design strategy that co-optimizes the freeform multilayer geometry and fully continuous layer-specific director distributions, and subsequently translates the optimized fields into fabrication-ready DIW toolpaths through an automated manufacturing-aware pipeline. To bridge computation and realization, we develop an optimization-centered 4D printing approach with automated, fabrication-aware toolpath generation tailored for direct ink writing of LCEs. With the proposed design-to-fabrication paradigm, we experimentally realize architectures that exhibit complex, non-intuitive thermo-mechanical behaviors. Experiments achieve highly challenging prescribed functionalities beyond the reach of intuition-based approaches and show excellent agreement with numerical simulations across all samples. This work establishes a generalizable inverse design and physical realization of freeform programmable LCE systems, enabling function-oriented and optimization-driven intelligent LCE applications for next-generation soft robotic and responsive material engineering.

title: Collection-Date Assignment Redirects Answers in Temporal QA
author: Minsu Oh
Seunghui Jwa
Soo Kyun Kim
Yeo-Chan Yoon
abstract: A collection date records when a source revision was acquired, not when its contents changed. Can assigning this metadata redirect temporal question answering despite unchanged evidence? Swapping the question day and following day between two revisions lowers later-reference exact match (EM) by 37.6-51.4 percentage points across five open-weight LLMs on 595 Wikipedia pages, replicated on 128 disjoint pages. Previous-day swaps retain 29.0-39.6-point losses on 497 pages. Seven prompt variants, including explicit ignore-collection instructions and archived-revision provenance, retain the effect. Fictional answers and English month-name question dates show that remembered answers and identical date strings are unnecessary. Matched thinking reduces Qwen3.5's penalty from 30.1 to 11.1 points, while native reasoners vary. Two API LLMs show small Wikipedia swap effects and rarely shift to earlier answers on fictional records. Large swap-induced losses concentrate around the question date; swaps between distant dates have much smaller effects. Adding fields containing one observed acquisition date lowers EM relative to omission in three of five LLMs after correction. The diagnostic isolates metadata effects from changing evidence or missing the relevant revision, and provides a practical audit for temporal QA inputs.

title: Evidence-Grounded SLM Behavioral Prediction Architecture for Future Assistance Use
author: Adeyemi Adeseye
Aisvarya Adeseye
Hannu Tenhunen
Jouni Isoaho
abstract: Users often exhibit changes in interaction behavior before explicitly seeking assistance, enabling systems to anticipate future assistance use. This is especially important in high-stakes environments, where delayed assistance can have operational, financial, or safety consequences. However, conventional Large Language Models (LLMs) are often unsuitable for continuous on-device behavioral prediction because of their computational and memory demands. Behavioral patterns are also highly individual and device-specific, motivating local processing that preserves privacy and data sovereignty. Small Language Models (SLMs) offer a promising alternative, but their ability to reason reliably over low-level sequential interaction events remains underexplored. This study introduces Evidence-Grounded Local Behavioral Prediction (ELBP), a four-layer architecture combining deterministic interaction processing, dual-view behavioral representation, SLM-based prediction, and evidence verification with abstention. Three instruction-tuned models of 3B parameters or fewer were evaluated using raw, structured, dual-view, and complete ELBP configurations. The best-performing model, Qwen2.5-3B with ELBP, achieved a full-set F1-score of 0.80 and PR-AUC of 0.84, representing a 15.9\% relative improvement over raw-event prompting and 17.6\% over XGBoost, while full-set ECE decreased by 43.2\% relative to raw-event prompting. With evidence verification and abstention, selective F1 increased to 0.84 at 91\% coverage and evidence support reached 96\%. These results show that structured behavioral representation and evidence-verified selective prediction can improve the reliability of behavioral forecasting in SLMs.

title: Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO: Dynamic Clipping Using Action Confidence and Normalized Advantage Magnitude
author: Taha M. Mahmoud
Naima Kaabouch
abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains a popular on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm owing to its stability and ease of implementation. Its clipping threshold, however, is fixed, so every training sample receives the same trust-region width regardless of how reliable the corresponding policy update is. This work examines adaptive-clipping variants of PPO in which the constant clipping parameter is replaced by sample-dependent thresholds computed from policy and return statistics. The central method, Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO (PPO-DAZ3), sets the clipping interval for each sample from two signals: action confidence, given by the probability of the selected action under the current policy, and update confidence, given by the normalized advantage magnitude. The rest of the standard PPO training pipeline is left unchanged. Evaluation on three classic control benchmarks (LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1) indicates that adaptive clipping improves learning in some settings but not all. PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, the smooth advantage-based variant PPO-AZ3S leads on Acrobot-v1, and standard PPO stays competitive on CartPole-v1, suggesting that adaptive clipping is most beneficial on harder control tasks.

title: SWE-Shift: Evaluating Coding Agents in Evolving Workspaces
author: Victor Shea-Jay Huang
Rongqing Li
Zhangyue Yin
Kelong Mao
Yaqi Zhao
Xinyuan Wang
Yao Yin
Lirui Luo
Renrui Zhang
Hongsheng Li
abstract: Repository-level coding benchmarks largely assume that tasks and environments remain unchanged throughout execution. In software development, code, dependencies, runtime state, and requirements can change while an agent is still working. We introduce SWE-Shift, a benchmark for evaluating coding agents under such mid-execution changes. From the same saved history and workspace, a Clean continuation proceeds without intervention, while a matched Shifted continuation receives a task-relevant update. Success requires completing the current task, preserving still-valid work, and satisfying the applicable state and evidence checks. The benchmark contains 120 scenarios across 12 change families, each evaluated at nine scheduled intervention positions. We evaluate 17 coding-agent systems, all of which have lower Shifted than Clean success. GPT-6 Astra drops from 67.35% to 24.79%, with 20.34% paired success. Tool/session changes and stale evidence yield zero paired success across all systems. Late-position paired success is lower for some systems and higher for others. These results show that success on the unchanged task can coexist with failures to preserve work, recover state, or refresh evidence after an update.

title: Do VLAs Know They Will Fail? Interpretable Success and Failure Patterns in Physical AI Systems
author: Christian A. Rogers
Qian Lin
Daniel S. Brown
abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.

title: SOPO: Socratic Guided Policy Optimization for Span-Level Hallucination Detection
author: Jiawei Dong
Zilong Bai
Pengtian zhu
Peng Zhou
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have gained widespread adoption in various natural language processing tasks, but suffer from hallucination issues where they generate unfaithful or inconsistent content. While Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) has shown promising applications in reasoning tasks, its application to span-level hallucination detection is challenged by localization ambiguity, reward sparsity on hard examples, and uncontrolled length inflation. To address these issues, we introduce Socratic Guided Policy Optimization (SOPO), a multi-turn RL framework for robust hallucination detection. The key innovation of SOPO is a Socratic feedback mechanism, where a teacher model guides the reasoning trajectories during rollout by providing indirect hints inferred from the ground truth. This teacher-guided approach enables the model to generate more effective reasoning trajectories for hard examples, thus alleviating reward sparsity. Furthermore, we incorporate Turn-based Advantage Scaling to penalize verbosity bias, encouraging the model to develop efficient and autonomous reasoning capabilities. Empirical results on RAGTruth demonstrate that SOPO (4B) achieves state-of-the-art performance, surpassing leading proprietary models (e.g., GPT-5) and standard RL baselines, while obtaining higher reported mean scores than GRPO on four out-of-domain benchmarks, with mixed evidence against CAPO. We release our training and evaluation code alongside the 1.7B and 4B SOPO models at https://github.com/patsnap/SOPO.

title: DIAL-S2ST: Learning Latency Control for Simultaneous Speech-to-Speech Translation
author: Jeongsoo Choi
Junseok Ahn
Joon Son Chung
abstract: We propose DIAL-S2ST, a post-training method for learning inference-time latency control in simultaneous speech-to-speech translation models. Our approach reuses pretrained translation capabilities through self-distillation from lookahead predictions, while limiting the influence of large text distillation losses to account for the imitation gap. This provides supervision for earlier emission without paired target data or reward computation. To make the learned timing adjustable at inference, we jointly train a single LoRA adapter across scales with matched lookahead guidance. Experiments on French-to-English translation with Hibiki demonstrate that only 10 hours of source speech enable this adaptation, providing flexible latency control with a favorable quality-latency trade-off.

title: Democratizing LLM Training with the Edge: Challenges, Systems, and the Road Ahead
author: Ziyue Luo
Jiaxuan Cai
Cedric LeDenmat
Srijith Nair
Fatemeh Nourzad
Rohith Krishnan
Qinhang Wu
Jifan Zhang
Sungjae Lee
Zhe Li
Peiwen Qiu
Siddharth Shah
Rishabh Sharma
Sundararajan Srinivasan
Yinglun Xia
Xue Zheng
Zidong Liu
Bicheng Ying
Kaushik Chowdhury
Gauri Joshi
Yingbin Liang
Robert Nowak
Srinivasan Parthasarathy
Saurav Prakash
Balaraman Ravindran
Sanjay Shakkottai
Ness B.Shroff
Haibo Yang
Aylin Yener
Jia Liu
abstract: The growing computational power of modern GPU data centers has let a few industrial giants train and deploy large language models (LLMs) on massive amounts of data. Yet the sheer scale of these models and their training data makes centralized development increasingly hard to sustain, and at the same time shuts out smaller institutions that hold relevant private data but lack comparable infrastructure. In this paper, we organize our positions on distributed LLM training around the pretraining and fine-tuning paradigms, covering federated learning, split learning, and decentralized approaches, and we assess their readiness for geo-distributed settings with heterogeneous hardware and unreliable connectivity. We then present a {\em unified} system architecture built around a cloud-hosted parameter server that coordinates heterogeneous clients over outbound gRPC connections, reusing one communication, compression, and fault-tolerance stack for both pretraining and a family of fine-tuning methods. We validate the design with real geo-distributed experiments on GPT-2 Medium and Llama3-1B pretraining across multiple university sites, showing stable convergence under realistic conditions. Finally, we chart the road ahead, identifying open problems that span frontier model support, elastic fault tolerance, adaptive compression, federated alignment, privacy and trust, incentive design, and system--algorithm co-design, all of which must be addressed to make democratized LLM training a reality.

title: PEAR: Adaptive Advantage Reshaping for Perception and Exploration in Large Vision-Language Models
author: Junxin Wang
Yingfeng Luo
Xiangchen Song
Weiqiao Shan
Runsong Zhao
Xinyu Liu
Shunjie Xing
Yifu Huo
Dingyang Lin
Qiuyu Gu
Yongyu Mu
Chenglong Wang
Changliang Li
Jingbo Zhu
Tong Xiao
abstract: Effective multimodal reasoning requires a model to reliably utilize visual information while sufficiently exploring diverse reasoning paths. To achieve this goal, prior work combines visual dependency and token entropy to reshape sequence-level advantages, but scaling the contribution of token entropy by visual dependency can leave high-entropy tokens with low visual dependency underweighted, despite their important role in reasoning exploration. To address this limitation, we propose PEAR, an adaptive advantage reshaping method for improving perception and exploration in multimodal reasoning. PEAR retains visual dependency as the base signal and adds an entropy-based exploration gain only at high-entropy positions, with lower visual dependency leading to a larger additional gain. The fused signal is then mapped to positive token-level weights that reshape the sequence-level advantage. Experiments on Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B show that PEAR achieves the highest average performance among evaluated baselines across multimodal reasoning benchmarks, alongside leading results on textual reasoning and general multimodal benchmarks.

title: Angular Supervision for Visual Object Grounding in Autoregressive Vision-Language Models
author: Parsa Esmaeilkhani
Longin Jan Latecki
abstract: Autoregressive vision-language models (VLMs) struggle to ground generated text in the correct image regions, and existing explainability methods, such as attention maps and Logit Lens, often produce poor spatial explanations due to weak text-to-vision attention and sink tokens. We propose \textbf{Angular Relevance} ($R_L$), a simple visualization measure based on cosine similarity between visual token embeddings and unembedding-matrix rows. Because $R_L$ is invariant to token norm, it produces substantially sharper and more faithful heatmaps than attention maps or Logit Lens on out-of-the-box models. Without any training, $R_L$ yields competitive referring-expression segmentation (RES), outperforming prior diagnostic maps and CLIP-based training-free methods. To preserve localized object information during cross-modal mixing, we introduce \textbf{Angular Object-Aware Loss (AOL)}, an auxiliary loss that directly supervises visual token embeddings to align angularly with the vocabulary directions of their corresponding object concepts. Finetuning with AOL alongside the standard next-token prediction objective significantly sharpens object localization in heatmaps, showing that the VLM's own visual tokens can be used directly for grounding and improving RES, without training any segmentation heads and without degrading general VQA performance. We further demonstrate that the learned grounding also transfers to category-level segmentation of object categories not seen during training.

title: ACWM-RM: A Reference-Free Reward Model from Complementary Mismatch Preferences
author: Shibo Hong
Siyu Ren
FengJiao Chen
Zhongyuan Peng
Wei Shi
Yixin Cao
abstract: Reinforcement learning has gained attention for improving action-conditioned world models (ACWMs), as it enables reward-driven optimization of visual quality (VQ) and action-following fidelity (AF) beyond flow-matching optimization. Realizing this potential requires reward signals that reliably rank videos by both VQ and AF. However, existing rewards capture only one dimension: metric-based rewards assess VQ but require ground-truth videos and do not directly assess AF, while inverse dynamics model (IDM) rewards assess AF without references but do not guarantee VQ. Moreover, IDMs, typically trained on real videos, may provide unreliable rewards for generated videos containing visual artifacts and physical inconsistencies. In this work, we introduce the Action and Video Mismatch Benchmark (AVM-Eval), comprising 67.2k pairs that evaluate how reliably IDMs assess AF on real and generated videos. We then propose ACWM-RM, a reward model that jointly assesses VQ and AF without ground-truth videos during reward computation. To train it, we first construct the Action and Video Mismatch Preference Dataset (AVM-Pref) with 506.3k pairs providing complementary supervision: action-mismatch pairs supervise AF, while video-mismatch pairs supervise VQ and expose the model to generated videos. We then pretrain an action-conditioned predictor on real videos to learn forward dynamics before jointly training it with a patch-weighted score head on AVM-Pref to transfer these dynamics to AF assessment on generated videos. Evaluation on AVM-Eval reveals the limited reliability of IDMs on generated videos, while downstream RL experiments show that ACWM-RM outperforms reward baselines in both criteria.

title: Correct Answers, Closed Gates: SolveBind for GUI Agents at the Verification Barrier
author: Xinhao Song
Haoxuan Peng
Su Su
Hongliang Wu
Sirui Song
Gongshen Liu
Linfeng Zhang
Dongrui Liu
abstract: Websites and applications deploy CAPTCHAs and anti-automation mechanisms that use behavioral signals such as interaction trajectories and timing, not outcomes alone, to distinguish humans from automated agents. We call these protected GUI environments, where correctly solving a verification task is insufficient for end-to-end task completion. Agents must turn solver outputs into accepted interactions and adapt execution to runtime feedback under time constraints.
